Only a handful of mountains on Earth count as true giants, and one small Himalayan country holds more of them than anyone else. Some stand on its borders with China and India; a few rise entirely inside it. The tallest of all is measured to the metre by both countries that share it.

research.topic: Eight-thousanders (peaks above 8,000 m): there are 14 on Earth, all in the Himalaya and Karakoram. Nepal contains or shares 8: Everest, Kangchenjunga, Lhotse, Makalu, Cho Oyu, Dhaulagiri, Manaslu and Annapurna. Pakistan has 5 (K2, Nanga Parbat, Gasherbrum I, Gasherbrum II, Broad Peak); China has 5 (Everest, Lhotse, Makalu and Cho Oyu shared with Nepal, plus Shishapangma entirely in Tibet). Of Nepal's eight, Everest, Lhotse, Makalu and Cho Oyu stand on the China border and Kangchenjunga on the India border; Dhaulagiri, Manaslu and Annapurna rise entirely inside Nepal. Everest's height was jointly announced by Nepal and China in December 2020 as 8,848.86 m. The southern approach starts from the Tenzing-Hillary airstrip at Lukla.

myths.myth: The highest mountains are spread evenly along the Himalaya, so no single country has many.
myths.reality: Nepal alone holds or shares eight of the fourteen eight-thousanders; Pakistan and China have five each, India one (shared).
